page: Microsoft Azure F80als_v7 is a compute-optimized virtual machine belonging to the Falsv7 family, powered by the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor. It features 80 dedicated physical cores and 80 vCPUs on an x86_64 architecture, utilizing the AMD EPYC 9V45 processor running at a clock speed of 4.5 GHz. The CPU configuration allocates 1.0 thread per core, ensuring dedicated execution resources without simultaneous multithreading. It is equipped with 160.0 GB of system memory, yielding a low memory-to-core ratio of 2.0 GB per vCPU. The processor includes a cache hierarchy of 48 KB L1d, 1.0 MB L2, and 32 MB L3 cache, alongside support for advanced vector extensions such as AVX-512 and cryptographic acceleration flags like AES and SHA_NI. No local storage is bundled with this instance, though it is premium storage capable, and it does not include any GPUs or complimentary public IPv4 addresses.

In benchmark evaluations, the F80als_v7 demonstrates top-tier performance, placing in the top 10% for both single-core and multi-core stress-ng CPU tests. This processing capability is supported by high-speed memory access, with cached small-block read bandwidth reaching 14244.96 GB/sec and uncached large-block read bandwidth at 477.47 GB/sec. Computational efficiency is reflected in top-tier scores for Passmark CPU metrics, including extended instructions, encryption, and physics simulations. The system also achieves top-tier throughput in data manipulation tasks, such as gzip compression and bzip3 decompression, alongside 199.48 million operations per second in Redis SET benchmarks. For language model execution, the instance processes prompts at 349.64 tokens per second on a medium 7B model, though text generation speeds for larger 70B models drop to a strong but lower 5.4 tokens per second.

The hardware profile presents a clear tradeoff between raw compute power and memory capacity. While the 4.5 GHz AMD EPYC processor delivers exceptional compute density, the 2.0 GB of RAM per core limits its suitability for memory-intensive database deployments or massive in-memory datasets. From a qualitative cost-efficiency perspective, this instance maximizes CPU resource allocation per dollar for compute-bound workloads, avoiding the added cost of unneeded memory or bundled local storage. It is structurally aligned for high-throughput batch processing, compute-heavy simulations, static web serving, and CPU-based machine learning inference where the memory footprint remains within the 160.0 GB boundary.
